"Nutritious" describes food or drink that is rich in nutrients — the substances your body needs to survive, grow, stay healthy, and function properly. Nutrients include things like proteins, vitamins, minerals, healthy fats, carbohydrates, and fiber. When a food contains plenty of these, it earns the label "nutritious."

Think of your body as a complex machine. To keep running well, it does not just need fuel to burn — it needs specific building blocks to repair itself, fight illness, and stay strong. Nutritious food provides exactly those building blocks.

Spinach is nutritious. It contains iron, calcium, vitamins A and C, and fiber — all things your body genuinely needs and uses. A donut, by contrast, is not nutritious. It may taste wonderful and give you a quick burst of energy from sugar, but it contains very few nutrients that your body can actually benefit from in a meaningful way.

"Nutritious" is a gradable adjective, meaning something can be more or less nutritious — it is not a simple yes-or-no quality. Brown rice is more nutritious than white rice because it retains more fiber and minerals. Kale is far more nutritious than iceberg lettuce. A meal made with vegetables, beans, and whole grains could be described as highly nutritious.

Several meanings are easy to confuse with "nutritious," so it is worth being precise about what the word does not mean.

It does not mean "delicious." A food can taste amazing but be completely lacking in nutrients — think of candy or chips. Equally, a food can be highly nutritious without being everyone's favorite in terms of taste.

It does not mean "filling." A food can make your stomach feel full without actually giving your body useful nutrients. Plain white bread may fill you up, but it is not very nutritious.

It does not mean "low-calorie." Some of the most nutritious foods in the world — avocados, nuts, salmon, olive oil — are also high in calories. Calories are simply units of energy. How nutritious a food is depends on what nutrients it contains, not on how many calories it has.

It does not mean "organic." Organic describes how a food was grown — without certain pesticides or synthetic chemicals. A food can be organic but not very nutritious, or deeply nutritious but not organic.

It is not identical to "healthy." These two words are close, but "healthy" is a much broader word. You can describe a person, a lifestyle, a habit, or a mindset as "healthy." "Nutritious" is used almost exclusively for food and drink — specifically to describe whether those foods are rich in the nutrients your body needs. You would say "a healthy person," not "a nutritious person."

Nourishing is the word most similar to "nutritious." Both describe food that gives the body what it needs. The difference is subtle: "nourishing" tends to carry a warmer, more personal or emotional quality — a nourishing bowl of soup feels caring and restorative. "Nutritious" sounds more factual and clinical — it is the word a doctor or nutritionist is more likely to use.

Wholesome is broader than both. It suggests food that is natural, pure, simple, and good in an honest sense. A wholesome meal feels right in a general, moral sort of way; a nutritious meal is specifically about being rich in the nutrients your body needs. These two words often overlap in practice, but they are not the same idea.

"Nutritious" is used almost exclusively with food and drink vocabulary: a nutritious meal, a nutritious diet, a nutritious snack, a nutritious drink, a nutritious recipe, nutritious ingredients. You cannot call a person, a city, a song, or a book "nutritious" in normal, literal usage — those would simply be wrong contexts for this word.

In everyday English, "nutritious" pairs naturally with certain words. You will frequently encounter phrases like highly nutritious, nutritious and delicious, a nutritious diet, a nutritious breakfast, quick and nutritious, and nutritious ingredients. Knowing these natural combinations will help you use and recognize the word confidently.

1. "Eggs are one of the most nutritious foods you can eat — they contain protein, healthy fats, and a wide range of vitamins."
  2. "She always makes sure her children have a nutritious breakfast before school."
  3. "Fast food is rarely nutritious because it tends to be low in vitamins and fiber and high in salt and unhealthy fats."
  4. "The doctor recommended a balanced, nutritious diet to support his recovery."
  5. "These smoothies are both delicious and nutritious."
  6. "Just because something looks natural or green does not automatically mean it is nutritious."
  7. "Lentils are surprisingly nutritious — they are packed with protein, iron, and fiber."

In short: if a food gives your body the substances it genuinely needs to work well and stay healthy, that food is nutritious. The more of those useful nutrients it contains, the more nutritious it is.
